steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting OpenMEDLab, an open-source platform for multi-modality foundation models in medicine. Explain why foundation models are hard to train and adapt for medical data, the main adaptation approaches, what the platform offers, and how the rest of the paper is organized.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Rise of foundation models and the data bottleneck in medicine
2. Adapting general foundation models with prompts / few-shot learning
3. Limits of direct finetuning; domain adaptation and medical foundation models
4. OpenMEDLab and its features
5. Outlook and paper organization

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Foundation models and medicine
- surge of deep learning foundation models in NLP and computer vision
- milestones: ViT, GPT, CLIP, SAM
- bigger models -> more capacity, more data needed (scaling law)
- medicine: shortage of public data and quality annotations = bottleneck
- many learning paradigms explored beyond finetuning pre-trained models (e.g. ImageNet pre-trained) with labeled domain data

2. Adapting existing foundation models
- model adaptation for medical downstream tasks using foundation models from other domains
- prompt engineering + cloud-deployed large-scale models (parallel computation, worldwide network) now a reality
- foundation model trained on thousands of millions of multi-modality data as base; single or few cases as prompts
- providing a few differentiable sample cases is feasible; matches training of medical residents, laboratory trainees
- few-shot methods use distinctive representations; succeeded in language modeling and vision
- fits long-tailed scenario: few rare disease cases

3. Finetuning and its limits
- medical data vary in format, source, modality, characteristics; general representations may not cover domain features
- so direct finetuning per downstream task still popular; uses labels, supervised
- drawback: tedious, time-consuming hand-labeling of volumetric data; attempts with weak labels, contextual info from longitudinal data
- extra adaptation step adjusting generalist representations with domain knowledge
- pioneering medical generalist/foundation models: BioGPT, MedSAM, PLIP
- needs unlabeled target-domain data: larger, easier to obtain
- ideally a repository hosting models, data, training/adaptation/benchmarking code

4. OpenMEDLab
- Fig. 1; open-source platform sharing medical foundation models in multi-modalities: imaging, NLP, bioinformatics, protein
- recruits solutions for building and adapting foundation models in medicine
- novel approaches for clinical/research tasks; lower cost, higher efficiency, better generalizability
- adapting foundation models -> efficient cross-domain, cross-modality diagnostic solutions
- features: world's first open-source platform for medical foundation models; 10+ data modalities; pioneering works (models, code, data); large-scale datasets; collaboration of top medical institutes

5. Outlook
- resource and demonstration for constructing/adapting foundation models for medical image analysis
- motivate shift from conventional transfer learning to foundation models and prompt learning
- following sections: prompting foundation models for medical image analysis, pre-trained medical image foundation models, medical LLMs, foundation models for downstream clinical applications

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recently deep learning foundation models have become very popular, especially in natural language processing and computer vision. Many milestone works have been proposed, like Vision Transformers (ViT), Generative Pretrained Transformers (GPT), Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP), and Segment Anything (SAM). As these models get bigger (in number of parameters), their capacity increases, but the amount of data needed for training also increases, following the scaling law. But in specific domains like medicine, the lack of public data and quality annotations has been the bottleneck for training large-scale deep learning models. So many learning paradigms have been researched to get around this, besides the usual routine of finetuning the pre-trained model (e.g., ImageNet pre-trained models) with domain-specific labeled data.

One straightforward solution is to build model adaptation techniques for medical downstream applications using the existing foundation models from other domains. This is especially true now that techniques like prompt engineering with cloud-deployed large-scale foundation models (with highly paralleled computation and worldwide network capacity) are becoming a reality. Here, a foundation model, which is often trained with thousands of millions of multiple modalities of data, could be the base for building medical applications with a single or a few cases given as prompts. It is more feasible to provide a few differentiable sample cases from a real-world scenario for model adaptation, and this is also similar to how professionals in the biomedical field are trained, e.g., medical residents and laboratory trainees. Few-shot methods could rely more on the distinctive representation from the foundation models, which has worked in many language modeling and vision tasks. It also fits the long-tailed scenario well, when only a few rare disease cases are available for training.

- medical data vary in format, source, modality, characteristics; general representations may not cover domain features

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recently deep learning foundation models have become very popular, especially in natural language processing and computer vision. Many milestone works have been proposed, like Vision Transformers (ViT), Generative Pretrained Transformers (GPT), Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP), and Segment Anything (SAM). As these models get bigger (in number of parameters), their capacity increases, but the amount of data needed for training also increases, following the scaling law. But in specific domains like medicine, the lack of public data and quality annotations has been the bottleneck for training large-scale deep learning models. So many learning paradigms have been researched to get around this, besides the usual routine of finetuning the pre-trained model (e.g., ImageNet pre-trained models) with domain-specific labeled data.

One straightforward solution is to build model adaptation techniques for medical downstream applications using the existing foundation models from other domains. This is especially true now that techniques like prompt engineering with cloud-deployed large-scale foundation models (with highly paralleled computation and worldwide network capacity) are becoming a reality. Here, a foundation model, which is often trained with thousands of millions of multiple modalities of data, could be the base for building medical applications with a single or a few cases given as prompts. It is more feasible to provide a few differentiable sample cases from a real-world scenario for model adaptation, and this is also similar to how professionals in the biomedical field are trained, e.g., medical residents and laboratory trainees. Few-shot methods could rely more on the distinctive representation from the foundation models, which has worked in many language modeling and vision tasks. It also fits the long-tailed scenario well, when only a few rare disease cases are available for training.

However, medical data can vary a lot in format, source, modality, and characteristics. The representations from foundation models (trained on more general data, e.g., natural images and free-text natural language corpus) may not cover the domain features well. This is also why directly finetuning the foundation models (or pre-trained models in a supervised way, e.g., ImageNet pre-trained models) for each downstream application is still popular. This usually uses labeled data and tunes the models in a supervised way. The aim is to solve individual downstream tasks using the strong representation learning and generalization abilities of foundation models. One big drawback is that it is a tedious and time-consuming job for medical professionals to hand-label volumetric data again and again, although there are attempts to use weak labels and contextual information from longitudinal data. So it could make more sense to add an extra adaptation step that adjusts the representation from generalist foundation models based on domain knowledge. There are also pioneering works on learning medical generalist/foundation models, e.g., BioGPT, MedSAM, PLIP. This process needs unlabeled data from the target domain, which is often much larger in quantity and easier to get. Ideally there would be a repository that hosts all the models, data, and cutting-edge code for model training, adaptation, and benchmarking, and showcases them as a better foundation for the various downstream clinical applications and research.

Here we present OpenMEDLab, shown in Fig. 1, an open-source platform for sharing medical foundation models in multi-modalities, e.g., medical imaging, medical NLP, bioinformatics, protein, etc. It also recruits innovative solutions for building and adapting foundation models in medicine, including the kinds of methods described above. In particular, it aims to promote new approaches to frontline clinical and research tasks in medicine, and it also looks for solutions with lower cost, higher efficiency, and better generalizability in training medical AI models. The new learning paradigm of adapting foundation models to downstream applications makes it possible to efficiently develop innovative solutions for cross-domain and cross-modality diagnostic tasks. OpenMEDLab has several features:

- World's first open-source platform for medical foundation models

- 10+ medical data modalities for a variety of clinical and research problems

- Pioneering works of the new learning paradigm using foundation models, including pre-trained models, code, and data.

- Large-scale medical datasets for pre-training and downstream applications.

- A collaboration between top medical institutes and facilities

We believe the OpenMEDLab open-source platform will be a distinct resource and demonstration of how foundation models can be built and adapted for medical image analysis. This will motivate researchers to move from conventional transfer learning techniques toward the new learning paradigm of foundation models and prompt learning. In the following sections, we introduce the foundation models and techniques in OpenMEDLab, i.e., prompting foundation models for medical image analysis, pre-trained medical image foundation models, medical large language models, and foundation models for various downstream clinical applications.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recently, deep learning foundation models have become very popular, particularly in the fields of natural language processing and computer vision. As a result, many milestone works have been proposed, such as Vision Transformers (ViT) [1], Generative Pretrained Transformers (GPT) [2], Contrastive Language-Image Pretraining (CLIP) [3], and Segment Anything (SAM) [4]. As the size (number of parameters) of these models grows bigger, the capacity of the models increases while the requirement of assembled data for training also grows, following the scaling law [5]. However, for specific domains like medicine, the shortage of public availability and quality annotations has been the bottleneck for training large-scale deep learning models. Therefore, a variety of learning paradigms has been researched to overcome the roadblock besides the conventional and monotone routine of finetuning the pre-trained model (e.g., ImageNet pre-trained models [6]) using domain-specific data with labels.

One straightforward solution is to develop model adaptation techniques for medical downstream applications by leveraging the existing foundation models from other domains, especially when techniques like prompt engineering with the availability of cloud-deployed large-scale foundation models (in both highly paralleled computation and worldwide network capacity) become a reality. In this case, a foundation model, often trained with thousands of millions of multiple modalities of data, could serve as the base for building medical applications with a single or a few cases in the form of prompts. It is more feasible to provide such a few differentiable sample cases from a real-world scenario for the model adaptation, and it also complies with the training process of professionals in the biomedical field, e.g., medical residents and laboratory trainees. Few-shot methods could leverage more on the distinctive representation produced by the foundation models, which has succeeded in considerable language modeling [7] and vision [8,9] tasks. It also fits well for the long-tailed scenario when only a few rare disease cases are available for the training.

Nevertheless, medical data could vary greatly in format, source, modality, and characteristics. Representations from the foundation models (trained with more general data, e.g., natural image and free-text natural language corpus) may not cover the domain features seamlessly. That’s also why finetuning the foundation models (or pre-trained models in a supervised way, e.g., ImageNet pre-trained models) for each downstream application directly remains popular. It usually employs data with labels and tunes the models in a supervised fashion. They aim to solve individual downstream tasks by utilizing the robust representation learning and generalization abilities of foundation models. One of the major drawbacks is that it remains a tedious and time-consuming job for medical professionals to hand-label volumetric data repeatedly, although attempts are made to utilize weak labels [10] and contextual information from the longitudinal data [11]. Therefore, adding an additional adaptation step could make more sense by adjusting the representation from generalist foundation models according to the domain knowledge [12]. Moreover, there are also pioneering works toward learning medical generalist/foundation models, e.g., BioGPT [13], MedSAM [14,15], PLIP [16]. This process requires unlabeled data from the target domain, which are often much larger in quantity and relatively easier to obtain. Ideally there would be a repository to host all the models, data, and cutting-edge model training, adaptation, and benchmarking codes and showcase them as a better foundation for the various downstream clinical applications and research.

Here, as shown in Fig. 1, we present OpenMEDLab, which is an open-source platform to share medical foundation models in multi-modalities, e.g., medical imaging, medical NLP, bioinformatics, protein, etc. Additionally, it recruits innovative solutions in building and adapting foundation models in medicine, including the category of methodologies introduced above. Particularly, it targets promoting novel approaches to frontline clinical and research tasks in medicine, and meanwhile, it seeks solutions to achieve lower cost, higher efficiency, and better generalizability in training medical AI models. The new learning paradigm of adapting foundation models to downstream applications makes it possible to develop innovative solutions for cross-domain and cross-modality diagnostic tasks efficiently. OpenMEDLab is distinguished by several features:

- • World’s first open-source platform for medical foundation models

- • 10+ medical data modalities targeting a variety of clinical and research problems

- • Pioneering works of the new learning paradigm using foundation models, including pre-trained models, code, and data.

- • Large-scale medical datasets for pre-training and downstream applications.

- • A collaborated work from top medical institutes and facilities

We believe that the OpenMEDLab open-source platform will serve as a distinct resource and demonstration of how foundation models can be constructed and adapted for medical image analysis purposes. This will motivate researchers to transition toward the novel learning paradigm of foundation models and prompt learning from the conventional transfer learning techniques. In the following sections, we will introduce the foundation models and techniques included in OpenMEDLab, i.e., prompting foundation models for medical image analysis, pre-trained medical image foundation models, medical large language models, and foundation models for various downstream clinical applications.
